title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
story:
By the time the Yadava clan — Krishna's own people — had all but destroyed itself, almost no one was left at his side. He had watched the working of his own maya, the great play of the world that he himself had set going, run out to its end. Now he walked down to the bank of the river Sarasvati, sipped its water, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree, the great sacred fig.

There he told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north. Uddhava, the companion who had followed Krishna all his life, found that he could not leave his feet. It was not that he meant to defy the command; it was that the road north led away from Krishna, and that was the one road Uddhava had never learned to take. He lingered, followed at a distance, and waited. Krishna found him there and said: "I know what your heart desires. I grant you what is hard for others to attain."

Uddhava has left his own account of that hour. He saw Krishna seated alone, deep in thought — the one he had sought and loved all his life. Krishna was dark and radiant, free of passion, his eyes peaceful and touched with red, his right foot resting on his left thigh. When Krishna spoke, Uddhava — the friend of the sage Vyasa — bowed low with joy.

"This is your last birth," Krishna told him. "My grace has come to you. What I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation — that is what I give you now."

Uddhava could barely take it in. He had asked for nothing; he had only failed to walk away when he was told to go. Now he was to receive what Krishna had spoken to Brahma at the dawn of the universe. He praised Krishna — the one who acts with no desire of his own; whose birth, and his being before all birth, alike pass all telling; the refuge of the sorrowing, to whom the frightened run from every fear; the one the sacred chants call upon, whose knowledge of himself is whole and unbroken and eternal; the one who, holding the secret of the self, could unfold it fully to another.

All his life, Uddhava saw now, he had been blessed, moment by moment, by Krishna's grace; only at this hour did he understand how much had already been given him. For one who served Krishna's feet, nothing was hard to obtain — not even the four aims men spend their lives seeking: duty, wealth, pleasure, and freedom.

And so, to Uddhava, whose heart lay open, Krishna taught the knowledge of the self, and granted him the state that is hard for others to attain.

It was the final teaching, given at the foot of a tree on the bank of a river, to the one man who could not make himself leave Krishna's feet. The world would long remember the words spoken at Kurukshetra; what Uddhava carried away that day was what came after them — the knowledge of the self, given quietly by a river.
reflection: Uddhava is told to go, and his reward is that he cannot; he receives the supreme state not for asking but for refusing to leave Krishna's feet. The episode quietly suggests that the last grace comes to those who cannot bear separation, even when the Lord himself sends them away.
tradition_note: The account in the third canto is Uddhava's own recollection of the moment; the fuller exposition of the teaching he received is traditionally known as the Uddhava Gita.
locations: the foot of an ashvattha tree
next_story_tease: Krishna's grace had one more errand for Uddhava: a message of comfort to the people of Vrindavan.
